title: Why intention matters more than attention | Pinterest Newsroom
summary: Marketers should focus on intention, not attention—helping consumers move seamlessly from digital discovery to meaningful offline actions.
body_markdown:
# Why intention matters more than attention


October 13, 2026


— Claudine Cheever, CMO, Pinterest


[Ads](https://newsroom.pinterest.com/news?filters=ads#news)


For years, the marketing industry has obsessed over time spent. We have treated every minute glued to a screen as a victory, regardless of what people were actually getting out of it. An entire generation is waking up to the true cost of being perpetually connected to a screen.


The pursuit of attention is no longer cost-free with 40% of US Gen Zers wishing social media was never invented.1 Three in five millennials and seven in ten Gen Zers in the US believe they spend too much time on their smartphones.2 In Europe and elsewhere, the picture is just as striking: 84% of 18 to 24 year-olds in Germany say they use their phones too much.3 47% of 16 to 21 year-olds in the UK say they would prefer to be young in a world without the internet.4


People are now actively choosing phones down and eyes up. We have seen a 567%5 global jump in phone-free events, alongside a 913% increase in US attendance,6 even on major concert tours like Phoebe Bridgers, who encourages fans to lock away their phones and be present for the show.


We call this tension "The Great Unplugging". It’s not just a rejection of the toxicity of social media; it’s a recognition of a life left unlived. We are seeing a rising awareness that digital experiences in isolation demand too much. We are seeing a clear expectation that online platforms must give people real world value in return.


The opportunity is clear. We can build a better version of online: one that helps people connect, discover and create without taking them away from their real lives.


Our latest research with Truth Be Told Consulting and Morning Consult across six global markets reveals a stark dichotomy in user behavior: "Scroll Mode" versus "Action Mode".


#### **The trap of the infinite feed**


We found that people pick up their devices with specific intent roughly 60%7 of the time, reaching for tools to help them solve problems, plan or create. Yet nearly half the time, that intent is hijacked. 44%8 of the time, people report getting sucked into passive scrolling when they did not intend to and feel trapped in the digital loop.


This passive consumption creates ad fatigue, not brand affinity. People are actively seeking the opposite: Pinterest search trends show massive spikes for "things to do instead of scrolling"9 (+365%),10 "analog aesthetic" (+260%),11 "dumb phone" (+150%),12 and real-world activities like nature film photography (+210%)13 and charcuterie board pottery (+676%).14


#### **The power of intent fulfilled**


Intention craves active discovery and content that helps users make decisions and take steps in their real lives.


When advertisers help feed and fulfill that intent, brand relationships transform completely. Brands achieve higher trust (+9%)15 and stronger purchase intent (+8%),16 whereas in passive scroll spaces people often ignore them (-8%).17


When you help build a bridge from the digital to the real, a brand is not an interruption, it is a useful part of the journey. The strongest brand experiences do not leave people asking, “What should I look at next?” They leave people ready to try, buy or do next.


#### **Designing for the exit**


The goal is not to hold attention captive, but to make the time spent useful enough to move people forward.


For marketers, success must be evaluated by customer progress made, not screen time captured. We must ask what that attention enables: Did it create intent? Build confidence? Prompt a decision? Help someone take a meaningful step offline?


This is where Pinterest sits, at the intersection of inspiration and utility. By matching consumer taste with active discovery, 73% of Pinterest users report that platform-inspired actions feel authentic, and 71% say those actions bring them closer to a life they love.18


When Sharpie launched its Creative Marker line, they chose Pinterest as they didn't just want to capture attention, they wanted to meet consumers in the intention economy. By pairing full-funnel targeting with frictionless ecarting during high-intent seasonal moments like Mother’s Day and back-to-school, they bridged the gap between online discovery and commerce, taking shoppers seamlessly from inspiration straight to their carts at Target, Walmart and Amazon. The commercial impact speaks for itself: a 4.93% incremental sales lift, 644% above the category median, with 74% of those incremental sales driven by completely new buyers.19


#### **The path forward**


The intention economy is here. Passive scrolling is a diminishing asset, and the real value for brands lies in the space where inspiration meets intent. The winning strategy is helping people move from discovery to decision, and from decision to action. It’s time we shift our focus from being the reason someone stays online to being the reason they go offline.


Read more on the[Pinterest Business Blog](http://business.pinterest.com/en-us/blog/design-the-exit?change_language=true) and download our playbook.
